The alleged victim said in a civil lawsuit this month she was drugged with ketamine, assaulted and raped in 2024 by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity, a social club for male students.
Cornell closed the fraternity and temporarily suspended the students involved, several of whom were later expelled.
The newly released details of the alleged incident have fuelled allegations that the university was too lenient and reignited a debate over sexual assault on U.S. campuses.
Matthew Van Houten, district attorney for Tompkins County in New York, said that he plans to file criminal charges against the seven men.
He said his office chose in 2024 not to prosecute because the victim’s testimony did not establish a lack of consent, but had now decided to do so in light of her latest allegations.
“I recognize the reality that it can take years of therapy and healing for victims of sexual assaults to fully process and understand what happened to them,” Van Houten said in a statement.
“Seeking justice sometimes requires us to reconsider or reopen cases when we are provided with additional evidence.”
Kyle Kimball, vice president of university relations at Cornell, said the Ivy League school supports the decision to reinvestigate the case.
He also rejected a claim, made in the civil lawsuit, that the suspects were offered the opportunity to write essays to mitigate their conduct.
“Any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false,” Kimball said.
The 101-page civil lawsuit filed in New York gives graphic details on the alleged assault of the woman, whose identity is being protected.
Notably, it provides a screenshot of a Snapchat group message advertising “free pussy” during the incident, apparently an invitation for other fraternity members to take part.
The suit seeks financial damages from Cornell and the seven suspects, adding that the woman has suffered “severe emotional and psychological distress.”
British actor Florence Pugh has voiced her anger about the case, saying she felt “uneasy and sick and anxious” after hearing about it.
“Colleges/schools/universities repeatedly fail women around the world,” she wrote on Instagram.
“You build men that get taught through time and time again that they can do extreme harm and that they won’t be harmed in return,” Pugh said.
Prominent Democratic lawmaker Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez condemned a “culture of rape” at elite institutions like Cornell.
“Jane Doe, that survivor, lost her education because you can’t stay in school when something like that happens to you,” Ocasio-Cortez said Sunday.
“She had to lose her education, and those men were protected by an institution and granted an Ivy League degree as a reward. Never again.”

deduped_items.title: Guanajuato will host a free outdoor Mexican-French circus spectacle this weekend as Cervantino Festival approaches
deduped_items.summary: Thousands of Guanajuato residents and visitors will be looking upward from the historic city center Saturday night as acrobats and tightrope walkers perform at high altitude in a spectacular joint effort by Mexican and French circus personnel. The post Guanajuato will host a free outdoor Mexican-French circus spectacle this weekend as Cervantino Festival approaches appeared first on Mexico News Daily
deduped_items.body_text:
Acrobats and tightrope walkers will turn Guanajuato’s historic city center into an open-air circus Saturday night, performing high above the crowd in a free opening-day show at the 54th International Cervantino Festival.
“Vértigo” — a Mexico-France collaboration adapted from the French production “Vertige” — is scheduled for 9 p.m. Saturday in Plaza Allende, the small square beside the Cervantes Theater in the historic city of Guanajuato.
The 60-minute show will combine aerial circus, dance, live music and a site-specific visual design.
The spectacle will bring together artists from Chaillot, a Paris-based national theater, and Mexican performers. Some of the acrobats and aerial balance artists (aka highliners) are affiliated with Mexico City’s Cirko de Mente.
Created by choreographer Rachid Ouramdane, musician Christophe Chassol and highliner Nathan Paulin, “Vértigo” adapts a piece first staged last year at the Grand Palais inaugural festival in Paris.
It was conceived as a mobile work, with performers suspended high above a public space and moving along tensioned lines.
The Guanajuato version was developed with Andrea Peláez, co-founder of the Mexico City contemporary-circus company Cirko de Mente, and Mexican artists.
France is the festival’s guest country this year, as part of a program marking 200 years of diplomatic relations with Mexico. The initiative recently yielded an exchange of centuries-old Aztec documents known as codices.
France’s program will include 18 presentations spanning classical and contemporary music, theater, dance, cabaret, street art, film, opera and multidisciplinary work.
The aerial circus is free, but overall, the Cervantino Festival mixes ticketed events with free events and free-access areas. It will run from Saturday, Oct. 3 through Sunday, Oct. 18.
Featuring more than 200 performances by some 2,750 artists, the event will include headliners such as Mike Patton’s Italian-song project Mondo Cane, which will open the festival at 7 p.m. Saturday.
The lineup also includes Australia’s Bangarra Dance Theatre, the German contemporary-music ensemble Ensemble Modern, Colombian salsa band Grupo Niche and Austria’s Camerata Salzburg with Spanish violinist María Dueñas.
One highlight will be an Oct. 15 tribute to the late José Alfredo Jiménez, the Guanajuato-born ranchera songwriter who wrote enduring Mexican standards including “El Rey” and “Si nos dejan.” Tenor Arturo Chacón Cruz and Mexico City-based Mariachi Gama 1000 will perform at the event at the Alhóndiga de Granaditas esplanade.
For more information, visit the festival’s official website.

deduped_items.title: Quinto campus de AMERIKE
deduped_items.summary: La universidad AMERIKE, que tiene como rectora a Cristina Peña, anunció la apertura de su quinto campus en México, ubicado en la zona corporativa de Santa Fe, con una inversión de 70 millones de pesos y una superficie de 4 mil metros cuadrados. La institución educativa busca atender la demanda de talento especializado en uno de los principales centros financieros e industriales de la capital del país, sumando esta nueva infraestructura a su red operativa en Guadalajara, Ciudad de México, Satélit

deduped_items.title: Diego Fischerman: “La canción argentina tiene una originalidad muy prodigiosa”
deduped_items.summary: Desde "El arriero" hasta "A estos hombres tristes", el experto encuentra en distintas canciones las claves de una identidad musical.Su nuevo ensayo combina crítica, memoria personal e investigación para recorrer intérpretes, compositores y géneros.Para el autor, las plataformas digitales amenazan con hacer desaparecer el espacio de descubrimiento que ofrece la radio.

deduped_items.title: How Rómulo Betancourt Allied with the US Without Surrendering Sovereignty
deduped_items.summary: In the 1960s, the Venezuelan president proved that democracy was a more sure bet for Washington's interests
deduped_items.body_text:
How Rómulo Betancourt Allied with the US Without Surrendering Sovereignty
In the 1960s, the Venezuelan president proved that democracy was a more sure bet for Washington's interests
John F. Kennedy receives Betancourt in the Oval Office on February 19, 1963. White House photograph by Abbie Rowe, JFK Presidential Library and Museum.
In 1898, the United States entered Cuba promising to liberate a nation; the subsequent occupation and the Platt Amendment ultimately granted it the right to intervene in the country’s affairs. A century before chavismo, Juan Vicente Gómez found a different formula: domestic order, foreign capital, and oil, all while leaving the citizenry out of the equation. Rafael Osío Cabrices and Marcus Golding have revisited both precedents to reflect on the Venezuela that would emerge after January 3. These two mirrors are uncomfortable, yet they are not the only ones; a third exists—also born of the relationship between Venezuela and the US—though it is based on a different idea of how to build stability.
During the 1950s, Venezuelan social democrat leader Rómulo Betancourt wrote from exile to convince Washington that its policy toward Latin America was based on a flawed premise. While military dictatorships might declare themselves anti-communist and guarantee a certain level of stability, repression, inequality, and a lack of civic participation paved the way for the very radicalization the US wished to contain. A democracy capable of enacting social reforms could serve as a more reliable ally.
This wasn’t Betancourt’s idea alone. Within the US government, there were already officials who viewed reformist forces as a more effective bulwark against communism. Betancourt’s own contribution lay elsewhere: articulating this argument from within Latin America and attempting to prove its validity while in power. Research by Steven Schwartzberg shows that this approach had begun even before the long exile triggered by the 1948 coup.
Upon returning to Venezuela after January 23, 1958, Betancourt did not ask the White House to build Venezuelan democracy. The major political parties agreed on rules for coexistence and the country held elections, which he won. His government undertook agrarian, educational, and social reforms starting in 1959, all while facing military conspiracies, guerrilla violence, and hostility from neighboring dictatorships. There were abuses, restrictions on civil liberties, and incomplete results. It was not a conflict-free democracy, but a democracy struggling to survive.
Both voting and finding a way out of the economic crisis remain priorities that oil alone cannot resolve.
That experience bolstered Betancourt’s argument before Washington. A State Department report from the time described Venezuela as a hemispheric leader in promoting social reform and economic development within a constitutional framework. This foreign alliance rested on a domestic political foundation: it did not rely solely on oil or on a shared stance against a common enemy.
The Cuban Revolution had made this discussion more urgent since January 1959. Upon arriving at the White House in 1961, John F. Kennedy understood that anti-communism alone was insufficient, and he found an exceptional partner in Betancourt. The Alliance for Progress sought to link development, social reform, and representative democracy. When Kennedy visited Venezuela in December 1961, the two governments issued a joint declaration framing economic cooperation within the context of “the effective practice of representative democracy.” Democracy was not a destination to be reached only when conditions became more favorable. It was an integral part of the journey itself.
1961 versus 2026
We can’t idealize that era. The Alliance for Progress yielded uneven results, and the US continued to tolerate dictatorships when it served its interests. Years later, Betancourt would welcome Jimmy Carter’s emphasis on human rights—as Guillermo Ramos Flamerich notes—

deduped_items.title: War and drought threaten world food security — 645m people at risk
deduped_items.summary: An estimated 645 million people worldwide face hunger. When disruptions occur, they reverberate far beyond an immediate conflict zone. The global food market faces the impact of Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, the war in the Middle East and the incoming El Niño. While everyone is affected, the most vulnerable countries, communities and persons are least able to absorb another shock to food prices and supplies.

deduped_items.title: Uganda: Prince Edward Rukidi Nyabongo I Is New Omukama of Tooro
deduped_items.summary: [Independent (Kampala)] Fort Portal, Uganda -- Prince Edward Rukidi Nyabongo I was installed early Tuesday morning as the new Omukama of Tooro in a series of traditional rituals held at Karuziika Palace in Fort Portal City. The traditional installation followed an overnight procession that began at 11 p.m. on Monday at Rwengoma Palace, with Nyabongo and thousands of his subjects walking about three kilometres through Fort Portal City to Karuziika Palace.
deduped_items.body_text:
Fort Portal, Uganda — Prince Edward Rukidi Nyabongo I was installed early Tuesday morning as the new Omukama of Tooro in a series of traditional rituals held at Karuziika Palace in Fort Portal City. The traditional installation followed an overnight procession that began at 11 p.m. on Monday at Rwengoma Palace, with Nyabongo and thousands of his subjects walking about three kilometres through Fort Portal City to Karuziika Palace.
The procession was illuminated by traditional lamps made from reeds as participants chanted, ululated and praised the incoming king. According to Kingdom protocol officials, the procession was conducted in accordance with traditional rules that barred women from participating in the overnight trek. The officials said the restriction applied only to the traditional ritual and that women were free to attend Tuesday's church service and public coronation.
The procession reached Karuziika Palace at about 3 a.m., where Nyabongo faced a traditional mock battle at Mugabante, the main entrance to the palace. Nyabongo's group battled an army led by Musuuga Charles Kamurasi in a ritual symbolising the incoming king's takeover of the royal seat. The ritual also included a fight with a bull, which was overpowered and killed.
Nyabongo emerged victorious, paving the way for him to enter the palace and continue with the traditional rituals reserved for a new Omukama. Members of the public who had accompanied Nyabongo stopped at Mugabante, while the new king and members of the royal family proceeded into the palace for private rituals. Inside Karuziika, traditional ritualists presented Nyabongo with the royal drums, including the main royal drum, Butwarane, which was sounded nine times.
Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines
TODAY'S Tooro coronation programme via @ubctvuganda pic.twitter.com/V6hlC8wZ8J -- The Independent (@UGIndependent) September 29, 2026
The sound of the drums triggered excitement among thousands of people gathered around the palace and marked a significant moment in the transition from the reign of the late Omukama Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV to the new king. Other rituals were performed inside the palace by Musuuga and traditional ritualists before Nyabongo was taken to the royal throne. He was also presented with royal regalia, including spears and a shield, as part of the traditional installation.
During the overnight rituals, royal regalia such as the spears and drums were restored to their upright positions after having been turned upside down following the death of Omukama Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV. The lion sculptures at the palace and in Fort Portal town were also uncovered, symbolising the end of the mourning period and the beginning of a new reign. The official coronation ceremony will begin on Tuesday with a church service at St. John's Cathedral in Fort Portal City.
According to the programme released by the Kingdom, Nyabongo left Karuziika Palace at 8:45 a.m. and is now at the cathedral, where Bishop Reuben Kisembo of Ruwenzori Diocese will lead the blessing service 9 a.m. to 10:30 a.m. Nyabongo will then return to Karuziika Palace for the formal coronation ceremony. President Yoweri Museveni is expected to attend the ceremony as the chief guest.

The traditional installation followed an overnight procession that began at 11 p.m. on Monday at Rwengoma Palace, with Nyabongo and thousands of his subjects walking about three kilometres through Fort Portal City to Karuziika Palace.
The procession was illuminated by traditional lamps made from reeds as participants chanted, ululated and praised the incoming king. According to Kingdom protocol officials, the procession was conducted in accordance with traditional rules that barred women from participating in the overnight trek. The officials said the restriction applied only to the traditional ritual and that women were free to attend Tuesday's church service and public coronation.
The procession reached Karuziika Palace at about 3 a.m., where Nyabongo faced a traditional mock battle at Mugabante, the main entrance to the palace. Nyabongo's group battled an army led by Musuuga Charles Kamurasi in a ritual symbolising the incoming king's takeover of the royal seat. The ritual also included a fight with a bull, which was overpowered and killed.
Nyabongo emerged victorious, paving the way for him to enter the palace and continue with the traditional rituals reserved for a new Omukama. Members of the public who had accompanied Nyabongo stopped at Mugabante, while the new king and members of the royal family proceeded into the palace for private rituals. Inside Karuziika, traditional ritualists presented Nyabongo with the royal drums, including the main royal drum, Butwarane, which was sounded nine times.

The sound of the drums triggered excitement among thousands of people gathered around the palace and marked a significant moment in the transition from the reign of the late Omukama Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV to the new king. Other rituals were performed inside the palace by Musuuga and traditional ritualists before Nyabongo was taken to the royal throne. He was also presented with royal regalia, including spears and a shield, as part of the traditional installation.
During the overnight rituals, royal regalia such as the spears and drums were restored to their upright positions after having been turned upside down following the death of Omukama Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV. The lion sculptures at the palace and in Fort Portal town were also uncovered, symbolising the end of the mourning period and the beginning of a new reign. The official coronation ceremony will begin on Tuesday with a church service at St. John's Cathedral in Fort Portal City.
According to the programme released by the Kingdom, Nyabongo left Karuziika Palace at 8:45 a.m. and is now at the cathedral, where Bishop Reuben Kisembo of Ruwenzori Diocese will lead the blessing service 9 a.m. to 10:30 a.m. Nyabongo will then return to Karuziika Palace for the formal coronation ceremony. President Yoweri Museveni is expected to attend the ceremony as the chief guest.

deduped_items.body_text:
Fort Portal, Uganda — Prince Edward Rukidi Nyabongo I was installed early Tuesday morning as the new Omukama of Tooro in a series of traditional rituals held at Karuziika Palace in Fort Portal City. The traditional installation followed an overnight procession that began at 11 p.m. on Monday at Rwengoma Palace, with Nyabongo and thousands of his subjects walking about three kilometres through Fort Portal City to Karuziika Palace.
The procession was illuminated by traditional lamps made from reeds as participants chanted, ululated and praised the incoming king. According to Kingdom protocol officials, the procession was conducted in accordance with traditional rules that barred women from participating in the overnight trek. The officials said the restriction applied only to the traditional ritual and that women were free to attend Tuesday's church service and public coronation.
The procession reached Karuziika Palace at about 3 a.m., where Nyabongo faced a traditional mock battle at Mugabante, the main entrance to the palace. Nyabongo's group battled an army led by Musuuga Charles Kamurasi in a ritual symbolising the incoming king's takeover of the royal seat. The ritual also included a fight with a bull, which was overpowered and killed.
Nyabongo emerged victorious, paving the way for him to enter the palace and continue with the traditional rituals reserved for a new Omukama. Members of the public who had accompanied Nyabongo stopped at Mugabante, while the new king and members of the royal family proceeded into the palace for private rituals. Inside Karuziika, traditional ritualists presented Nyabongo with the royal drums, including the main royal drum, Butwarane, which was sounded nine times.

deduped_items.summary: Aux portes d’Antananarivo, à Madagascar, la région de l’Itasy abrite de nombreuses exploitations maraîchères familiales. Alors que la croissance démographique impose d’augmenter la production agricole, les sols souffrent de l’érosion et sont appauvris à long terme par l’utilisation d’engrais chimiques. Mais depuis près de dix ans, des milliers de paysans ont adopté un biofertilisant liquide dans leurs pratiques agricoles, ce qui a permis d’améliorer les rendements tout en préservant l’environnem

deduped_items.title: Greater Manchester mayor Bev Craig vows to put ‘grown-up shoes’ on when hosting Donald Trump
deduped_items.summary: Craig — fresh from meeting Zohran Mamdani — says she will host the U.S. president at the G20 next year "in a professional and serious way."
deduped_items.body_text:
LIVERPOOL, England — Greater Manchester’s new progressive mayor Bev Craig is already getting on famously with Zohran Mamdani. Expect her dealings with Donald Trump to be a lot more businesslike.
Craig — fresh from a visit to New York to meet the mayor earlier this month — told the POLITICO Pub at Labour conference Tuesday she would put her “big shoes” on when Trump visits Manchester for the U.K.-hosted G20 summit next year, even if they disagree.
“I’m not sure that’s the bromance I’m after in my life,” the Labour politician said. “I think I’ll stick to Mamdani as my new U.S friend.”

UKMTO reports strike on vessel in Strait of Hormuz
29 September 2026 14:19 BST
  
  The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said on Tuesday that a vessel was hit by an apparent projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz on Monday evening, causing a fire.
The fire was later put out and the crew were all safe, with the vessel continuing its journey.

The attack comes as attacks continue around the strategic waterway, disrupting global shipping and keeping the heat on oil markets.

deduped_items.title: UK accused of 'fuelling' Yemen war as Saudi jets receive British support
deduped_items.summary: UK accused of 'fuelling' Yemen war as Saudi jets receive British support Submitted by Areeb Ullah on Tue, 09/29/2026 - 11:53 Academics and civil society groups warn British military assistance to Riyadh risks complicity in further violations as fighting escalates Wreckage of what Yemen's Houthi rebels said was a downed Saudi drone in Al-Jawf governorate, Yemen, 26 July 2026 (Ansarullah Media Center/AFP) Off The UK government faces calls to halt military support for Saudi Arabia as fighting escal
deduped_items.body_text:
UK accused of 'fuelling' Yemen war as Saudi jets receive British support
The UK government faces calls to halt military support for Saudi Arabia as fighting escalates in Yemen, with academics and civil society organisations warning that British refuelling for Saudi fighter jets could make it complicit in further violations of international law.
In an open letter addressed to Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, the signatories said they were “deeply concerned” about the decision to refuel Royal Saudi Air Force aircraft as hostilities escalate in and around Yemen.
“There is a real risk that further UK military support for Saudi Arabia will not achieve the desired outcome and could make the UK complicit in further war crimes and violations of international humanitarian law,” they wrote.
The Campaign Against Arms Trade, Action on Armed Violence, Shadow World Investigations UK and the Yemen Relief and Reconstruction Foundation signed the letter alongside academics and specialists in international relations, human rights and international law.
The signatories highlighted longstanding British support for Saudi military action in Yemen, which began in 2015 and initially involved a coalition of Arab states.

Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
The Yemen Data Project recorded 25,054 Saudi-led coalition air raids between 2015 and 2022, according to figures cited in the letter. The organisations said extensive evidence showed that the air campaign attacked civilians and civilian infrastructure.
The war also combined an air and sea blockade with economic collapse and ground fighting. The UN Development Programme estimated that the conflict killed 377,000 people directly and indirectly by the end of 2021, the letter said.
The signatories also cited allegations that the Saudi-led coalition used starvation as a weapon during the conflict.
'Risking complicity'
The groups argue that the Saudi-led intervention failed to defeat or dislodge the Houthis, who continued to control most of Yemen's population.
They also criticised Britain's role in US air strikes against the Houthis in spring 2025. The UK reportedly supported those operations by providing refuelling.
The signatories cited a Pentagon assessment that said the strikes between March and May 2025 “more likely than not” caused 281 civilian casualties.
The latest escalation has unfolded against a wider regional crisis.
The letter cites reports that fighting has displaced around 130,000 people in recent weeks. It also says the violence has already caused 110 casualties, including 28 deaths.
The signatories also raised concerns about Houthi attacks and attempted attacks on civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia.
They attributed the latest escalation to several factors, including developments inside Yemen, the US-Israeli war on Iran and the war in Gaza.
But the groups argue that more air strikes will not resolve the conflict.
“Past experience has shown that air strikes will not contribute to defeating the Houthis or alleviating pressure on Saudi Arabia or on global shipping routes,” they wrote.
“Instead, the UK is only further fuelling the war and is risking complicity in further crimes.”
'De-escalatory diplomacy'
The organisations called on the British government to stay out of Saudi military operations and pursue diplomatic efforts to de-escalate the conflict.

deduped_items.body_text:
Gaza officials warn of imminent 'humanitarian catastrophe' as winter approaches
Gaza’s Government Media Office has accused Israel of violating its commitments under the Gaza ceasefire agreement, saying the continued violations have worsened the humanitarian crisis as the ceasefire approaches its first anniversary.
Israel had committed 5,147 violations that killed 1,421 Palestinians, injured 4,983 and caused the arrest of 198 people, the office said.
It also said 72,826 aid trucks had entered Gaza of an expected 210,600 under the agreement, while only 13,785 people had been allowed to travel in and out of the territory of an expected 35,000.
As winter approaches, the office warned of a “certain humanitarian catastrophe” as more than 1.5 million displaced Palestinians live in worn-out tents.
It said 162,000 of Gaza’s estimated 270,000 tents were already unusable and warned that more than 255 damaged buildings were in danger of collapse.
The office appealed to the international community and the UN agencies to intervene urgently, fully open Gaza’s crossings, facilitate medical evacuations and allow winter relief supplies into the territory.

deduped_items.title: Bangladesh energy crisis calls for pragmatism, not political purity
deduped_items.summary: For more than three decades, the Bangladeshi political left has maintained an unyielding stance on natural resources like gas, coal, and minerals, insisting that state entities must develop them exclusively. Foreign energy companies are viewed with deep suspicion, while production-sharing contracts are routinely condemned as vehicles designed to siphon national wealth to foreign multinationals. deduped_items.body_text:
For more than three decades, the Bangladeshi political left has maintained an unyielding stance on natural resources like gas, coal, and minerals, insisting that state entities must develop them exclusively.
Foreign energy companies are viewed with deep suspicion, while production-sharing contracts are routinely condemned as vehicles designed to siphon national wealth to foreign multinationals. Coal extraction, particularly open-pit mining, has drawn even sharper resistance.
Few figures have championed this doctrine more consistently than economist Anu Muhammad and his National Committee to Protect Oil, Gas, Mineral Resources, Power and Ports. Their long-standing campaigns have influenced the nation’s media narrative on energy.
By transforming projects like the Phulbari open-pit coal mine into lightning rods for outrage, they have successfully framed energy deals with outside capital as existential threats to national ownership.
To be sure, their environmental objections warrant rigorous examination. The Phulbari dispute raised acute questions regarding mass human displacement, farmland destruction, groundwater depletion and ecological ruin.
As Anu Muhammad reaffirmed recently, resource extraction cannot be plausibly classified as development if it dismantles local agrarian economies, ecosystems and human habitations.
Yet the left’s stance becomes intellectually fragile when legitimate environmental advocacy hardens into an indiscriminate hostility toward foreign capital and technical expertise. Bangladesh can no longer afford to treat its national energy discourse as an abstract seminar or a street protest over political purity.
The country faces an acute energy crisis. Daily gas demand is around 3,800 to 4,000 million cubic feet, while domestic production provides barely 2,600 million. Shrinking domestic reserves have forced the state into dangerous over-reliance on imported liquefied natural gas (LNG).
This import dependency has proven very costly. Recent geopolitical volatility across Middle Eastern supply routes has pushed Asian spot LNG prices to eye-watering highs.
Bangladeshi manufacturers now endure persistent supply curtailments and rolling power outages, while the treasury absorbs sharp fiscal burdens. Over 40% of the nation’s power generation currently hinges on imported LNG, severely undercutting industrial expansion.
This is why the old dogma on foreign exploration must be re-evaluated. Left-wing commentators persistently offer BAPEX, the state-owned exploration entity, as a viable solution.
Strengthening state capabilities is undoubtedly a worthy goal; BAPEX possesses valuable localized geological insight, technical personnel and operational infrastructure. But bolstering a national oil company is fundamentally distinct from shutting out global energy corporations.
Consider deep-sea exploration in the Bay of Bengal. High-seas drilling demands immense capital expenditure alongside extreme financial risk. A single offshore exploratory well can easily absorb hundreds of millions of dollars without yielding any commercial discoveries.
While nationalizing that risk carries rhetorical political appeal, the state remains fully exposed when costly wells come up dry. International oil majors exist precisely because their global balance sheets can absorb such losses.
Bangladesh has spent years learning how challenging it is to lure global energy majors. Despite restructuring production-sharing terms to offer lucrative blocks across the Bay of Bengal, major tenders have repeatedly failed to attract a single international bid.
Rather than triggering a serious debate regarding contractual competitiveness, geological data sharing and regulatory predictability, public discourse predictably degenerated into binary slogans pitting national sovereignty against foreign exploitation.

deduped_items.body_text:
For more than three decades, the Bangladeshi political left has maintained an unyielding stance on natural resources like gas, coal, and minerals, insisting that state entities must develop them exclusively.
Foreign energy companies are viewed with deep suspicion, while production-sharing contracts are routinely condemned as vehicles designed to siphon national wealth to foreign multinationals. Coal extraction, particularly open-pit mining, has drawn even sharper resistance.
Few figures have championed this doctrine more consistently than economist Anu Muhammad and his National Committee to Protect Oil, Gas, Mineral Resources, Power and Ports. Their long-standing campaigns have influenced the nation’s media narrative on energy.
By transforming projects like the Phulbari open-pit coal mine into lightning rods for outrage, they have successfully framed energy deals with outside capital as existential threats to national ownership.
To be sure, their environmental objections warrant rigorous examination. The Phulbari dispute raised acute questions regarding mass human displacement, farmland destruction, groundwater depletion and ecological ruin.
As Anu Muhammad reaffirmed recently, resource extraction cannot be plausibly classified as development if it dismantles local agrarian economies, ecosystems and human habitations.
Yet the left’s stance becomes intellectually fragile when legitimate environmental advocacy hardens into an indiscriminate hostility toward foreign capital and technical expertise. Bangladesh can no longer afford to treat its national energy discourse as an abstract seminar or a street protest over political purity.
The country faces an acute energy crisis. Daily gas demand is around 3,800 to 4,000 million cubic feet, while domestic production provides barely 2,600 million. Shrinking domestic reserves have forced the state into dangerous over-reliance on imported liquefied natural gas (LNG).
This import dependency has proven very costly. Recent geopolitical volatility across Middle Eastern supply routes has pushed Asian spot LNG prices to eye-watering highs.
Bangladeshi manufacturers now endure persistent supply curtailments and rolling power outages, while the treasury absorbs sharp fiscal burdens. Over 40% of the nation’s power generation currently hinges on imported LNG, severely undercutting industrial expansion.
This is why the old dogma on foreign exploration must be re-evaluated. Left-wing commentators persistently offer BAPEX, the state-owned exploration entity, as a viable solution.
Strengthening state capabilities is undoubtedly a worthy goal; BAPEX possesses valuable localized geological insight, technical personnel and operational infrastructure. But bolstering a national oil company is fundamentally distinct from shutting out global energy corporations.
Consider deep-sea exploration in the Bay of Bengal. High-seas drilling demands immense capital expenditure alongside extreme financial risk. A single offshore exploratory well can easily absorb hundreds of millions of dollars without yielding any commercial discoveries.
While nationalizing that risk carries rhetorical political appeal, the state remains fully exposed when costly wells come up dry. International oil majors exist precisely because their global balance sheets can absorb such losses.
Bangladesh has spent years learning how challenging it is to lure global energy majors. Despite restructuring production-sharing terms to offer lucrative blocks across the Bay of Bengal, major tenders have repeatedly failed to attract a single international bid.
Rather than triggering a serious debate regarding contractual competitiveness, geological data sharing and regulatory predictability, public discourse predictably degenerated into binary slogans pitting national sovereignty against foreign exploitation.

For more than three decades, the Bangladeshi political left has maintained an unyielding stance on natural resources like gas, coal, and minerals, insisting that state entities must develop them exclusively.
Foreign energy companies are viewed with deep suspicion, while production-sharing contracts are routinely condemned as vehicles designed to siphon national wealth to foreign multinationals. Coal extraction, particularly open-pit mining, has drawn even sharper resistance.

By transforming projects like the Phulbari open-pit coal mine into lightning rods for outrage, they have successfully framed energy deals with outside capital as existential threats to national ownership.

deduped_items.title: إثيوبيا: لماذا عادت المواجهات في تيغراي؟
deduped_items.summary: سيطر الجيش الفدرالي الإثيوبي على ألاماتا، وهي أول بلدة مهمة في تيغراي يستحوذ عليها منذ تجدد المعارك مع فصائل مسلحة الأسبوع الماضي، وتأتي هذه التطورات الميدانية غداة اتهام قائد الجيش المشير برهانو جولا، إريتريا والسودان ومصر بدعم متمرّدي الإقليم الذي أعلنت سلطاته أنها تخوض "حربا شاملة" ضد حكومة أديس أبابا برئاسة آبي أحمد علي. ماذا تعني سيطرة القوات الموالية للحكومة على ألاماتا؟ وهل تمهد لتقدمها نحو ميكيلي؟ و ما حجم التدخل الخارجي في الصراع؟ للحديث عن هذا الموضوع نستضيف الباحث والكاتب في الشؤون ال

deduped_items.summary: سيطر الجيش الفدرالي الإثيوبي على ألاماتا، وهي أول بلدة مهمة في تيغراي يستحوذ عليها منذ تجدد المعارك مع فصائل مسلحة الأسبوع الماضي، وتأتي هذه التطورات الميدانية غداة اتهام قائد الجيش المشير برهانو جولا، إريتريا والسودان ومصر بدعم متمرّدي الإقليم الذي أعلنت سلطاته أنها تخوض "حربا شاملة" ضد حكومة أديس أبابا برئاسة آبي أحمد علي. ماذا تعني سيطرة القوات الموالية للحكومة على ألاماتا؟ وهل تمهد لتقدمها نحو ميكيلي؟ و ما حجم التدخل الخارجي في الصراع؟ للحديث عن هذا الموضوع نستضيف الباحث والكاتب في الشؤون ال
